content:
Today we enter Numbers chapter thirteen. Israel had now reached the wilderness of Paran. They had left Sinai and passed through the hard lessons of Taberah, Kibroth-hattaavah, and Hazeroth, and now they stood near the borders of the land Yahweh had promised to give them. The journey had brought them to a very important moment. They were not merely hearing about Canaan anymore. They were about to see the land with their own eyes.

Numbers 13:1-2 says, "The LORD now said to Moses, 'Send out men to explore the land of Canaan, the land I am giving to the Israelites. Send one leader from each of the twelve ancestral tribes.'" Yahweh told Moses to send men to spy out the land, one from each tribe, and these were not ordinary men. They were leaders among the people. They carried the honour of their tribes, and they were trusted to observe the land carefully and bring back a report. Among these twelve men, two names would later become very important; Caleb from the tribe of Judah, and Hoshea from the tribe of Ephraim, whose name Moses changed. Numbers 13:16 says, "Moses called Hoshea son of Nun by the name Joshua." Hoshea means salvation, but Joshua carries the meaning Yahweh is salvation, or Yahweh saves. This name would become very significant, because Joshua would one day be the very man to lead Israel into the land after Moses.

Moses gave the spies clear instructions. They were to go up through the Negev and into the hill country, and to see what the land was like; whether the people were strong or weak, few or many, whether the towns were open camps or fortified cities, and whether the land was rich or poor. Numbers 13:20 says, "Is the soil fertile or poor? Are there many trees? Do your best to bring back samples of the crops you see." Then the verse adds an important note about the timing: "It happened to be the season for harvesting the first ripe grapes."

This means the spies entered the land at a fruitful time. They were not seeing it in a dead and barren season. They saw it when the grapes were beginning to ripen. The land itself was ready to testify of Yahweh's goodness.

The spies went up and explored the land from the wilderness of Zin as far as Rehob, near Lebo-hamath. Then they passed through the Negev and came to Hebron. Hebron was an ancient and important city, and the bible tells us it had been founded seven years before Zoan in Egypt. Zoan was an old and famous Egyptian city, so this note shows us the great age of Hebron. But Hebron was also deeply important in the history of the fathers. Abraham had lived in that region. Sarah died there, and Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah near Hebron as a burial place. Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were all connected with that burial place. So when the spies came to Hebron, they were walking through a land already tied to the very promises Yahweh had made to Abraham. Yet Hebron was also the place where the descendants of Anak lived; Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai - tall and powerful people whose presence stirred fear in the hearts of the spies.

Then the spies came to the valley of Eshcol. Numbers 13:23 says, "When they came to the valley of Eshcol, they cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes so large that it took two of them to carry it on a pole between them! They also brought back samples of the pomegranates and figs." This is one of the most famous scenes in the whole chapter. The grapes were so large that one single cluster had to be carried on a pole between two men. They also brought pomegranates and figs, and these fruits became living proof that the land was fertile and good. The place itself was named after this cluster, for Numbers 13:24 says, "That place was called the valley of Eshcol, which means 'cluster,' because of the cluster of grapes the Israelite men cut there." The fruits of Canaan were not small. They were not poor. They were not disappointing. Yahweh had promised a good land, and the fruit itself proved it. The grapes, the pomegranates, and the figs were all witnesses. The land was truly flowing with blessing. Jewish tradition gives strong attention to this fruit, describing the cluster as unusually large and speaking of the men needing help to carry it. These traditions emphasise the very same point found in the biblical text; the land was exceedingly fruitful. Yet the spies would use even the greatness of the land to increase fear. What should have strengthened faith became, in their hands, part of a frightening report.

The spies spent forty days exploring the land. Forty days was enough time to see the land properly. They had seen the south and the north. They had seen the fruit, the cities, the people, and the strength of the land. When they returned, they came to Moses, Aaron, and all the congregation at Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran, and they brought back the fruit and gave their report. Numbers 13:27 says, "This was their report to Moses: 'We entered the land you sent us to explore, and it is indeed a bountiful country; a land flowing with milk and honey. Here is the kind of fruit it produces.'" At first, their report was entirely true. They admitted that the land was good. They said it truly flowed with milk and honey. They held up the fruit for all to see. Their eyes had seen exactly what Yahweh had promised.

But then came the one word that changed the tone of the whole report. Numbers 13:28 says, "But the people living there are powerful, and their towns are large and fortified. We even saw giants there, the descendants of Anak!" The land was good, but the people were strong. The fruit was real, but the cities were fortified. The promise was true, but the enemies looked great. And this is where the bad report began. Now the problem was not that they mentioned the facts. It was true that the cities were strong. It was true that powerful people lived there. It was true that the descendants of Anak were in the land. Their sin was that they spoke as though those things were greater than Yahweh's promise. They went on describing the peoples of the land; the Amalekites in the Negev, the Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites in the hill country, and the Canaanites along the coast and the Jordan Valley. Their report grew heavier and heavier with fear.

And at that moment, Caleb spoke. Numbers 13:30 says, "But Caleb tried to quiet the people as they stood before Moses. 'Let's go at once to take the land,' he said. 'We can certainly conquer it!'" Caleb did not deny the size of the enemies.

He did not pretend the cities were weak. But he believed Yahweh. He had seen the very same land, the same giants, the same fortified cities, and the same fruit as all the others. Yet his conclusion was completely different: we can certainly conquer it. This is the good report. The good report did not ignore the difficulty. The good report simply placed Yahweh's promise above the difficulty. But the other spies answered him. Numbers 13:31 says, "But the other men who had explored the land with him disagreed. 'We can't go up against them! They are stronger than we are!'" This was the very heart of unbelief. They measured themselves against the enemy, but they forgot to measure the enemy against Yahweh. If the battle depended only upon Israel's strength, then their fear would make perfect sense. But the land was never to be taken by Israel's strength alone. It was Yahweh who had promised to give it.

Numbers 13:32 says, "So they spread this bad report about the land among the Israelites: 'The land we traveled through and explored will devour anyone who goes to live there. All the people we saw were huge.'" This was no longer a careful report. It had become an exaggerated and faithless one. Earlier they had said the land flowed with milk and honey. Now they said the land devoured its inhabitants. Earlier they had shown the fruit. Now they made the land itself sound deadly. Fear had changed their words. Then they said, "We even saw giants there, the descendants of Anak. Next to them we felt like grasshoppers, and that's what they thought, too!" (Numbers 13:33).

Here we must explain something carefully. Some translations use the word Nephilim in this verse. But the Nephilim mentioned here in Numbers 13 should not be treated as the same group as the Nephilim of Genesis 6 who lived before the Flood. Genesis 6 speaks of the Nephilim in the world before the Flood, and that world was destroyed. Numbers 13 is much later, after the Flood, in the days of Moses. The ten spies used frightening language to describe the size and strength of the people in Canaan, connecting the Anakim with that terrifying name in order to make the people afraid. So we should not think that the exact same pre-Flood Nephilim survived and were living in Canaan. The more careful understanding is that the spies were using the name to describe giant-like warriors, especially the sons of Anak, and their goal was to magnify the danger and weaken Israel's faith. Deuteronomy also speaks of the Anakim as a tall and strong people, for Deuteronomy 9:2 says, "The people are strong and tall; descendants of the famous Anakite giants." So the men of Anak were truly tall and feared. But the fear-filled spies went far beyond the truth. They made Israel feel small and helpless, saying, "We felt like grasshoppers."

And so this is where the chapter ends; not with the fruit, but with fear; not with Caleb's faith, but with the people hearing a bad report. Numbers 13 gives us two reports from the very same land. The good report said: the land is good, Yahweh has promised it, and we are able to take it. The bad report said: the land is dangerous, the people are too strong, the cities are too great, and we cannot go up. Both groups saw the same grapes. Both groups saw the same cities. Both groups saw the same descendants of Anak. Both groups walked through the same land for the same forty days. But one group looked at the land through faith, and the other looked at it through fear. The land itself was exactly what Yahweh had said it would be. It was fruitful. It was rich. It had grapes, pomegranates, and figs. It was a land flowing with milk and honey. Yet the heart of man can turn even the proof of Yahweh's goodness into a reason for fear. The spies brought back fruit in their hands, but ten of them carried unbelief in their hearts. Caleb stood with faith and said, "Let us go up at once." The others said, "We are not able." This chapter prepares us for the serious events that follow in Numbers 14, for the report of the spies would not remain as words only. Their words would soon move the whole congregation to fear, to weeping, to rebellion, and to judgment.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

We thank You for showing us the goodness of the land You promised to Israel.

We thank You for the witness of the grapes, the pomegranates, and the figs.

Help us to read Your Word carefully and never to turn Your promises into fear.

Give us a heart like Caleb, that sees the difficulty but trusts Your promise above it.

Keep us from spreading fear among the brethren when You have already spoken good.

"When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you. I praise God for what he has promised." Psalm 56:3-4

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
